newsitem.title: GERMANY: No poison found so far in Nestle extortion probe. [CORRECTED 18:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: No poison found so far in Nestle extortion probe. [CORRECTED 18:45 GMT]

text.p: Food giant Nestle said on Wednesday it had so far found no sign of contamination in groceries pulled from supermarket shelves across Germany after extortionists said they had poisoned its products.
The extortionists said in a letter to the company they had poisoned products bearing the name of Nestle or its German subsidiary, Deutsche Thomy GmbH, in 55 stores in 14 cities.
Police believe the criminals were also behind two previous attempts to extort money from the firm over the past year.

The latest threat, which was made public on Tuesday evening, sparked a nationwide alert and more than 15,000 people flooded police with phone calls on an emergency number. Up to 80,000 called but were unable to get through, police said.
Investigators, who say they have no clues about the identity of the extortionists, cleared the shelves of products which could have been contaminated, such as mustard and mayonnaise.
"The good news is that there is no sign that any products have been contaminated," Nestle spokesman Winfried Peters said, adding that checks had been completed in 11 of the 14 cities.

The latest letter followed two earlier attempts to blackmail the company in August 1996 and in April this year, when police discovered two tubes of mustard laced with cyanide in two supermarkets in southern Germany.
Thomy said it lost some 30 million marks ($16 million) in removing and replacing products from store shelves in April.

Peters said it was too early to quantify the financial cost of pulling the products this time. "Like the last time, there will certainly be a fall in turnover but we're optimistic that it won't be as pronounced as the last time," he said.
Police declined to say how much money the extortionists were demanding but ZDF television, citing anonymous sources, said they wanted $15 million in uncut diamonds.
The letter also said that, four weeks ago, 23 packages of poisoned Nestle products had been left in public areas such as parks, trams, buses, train stations and phone booths.
The blackmailer claimed to have left packages in cities such as Berlin, Bremen, Chemnitz, Dortmund, Dresden, Frankfurt, Hamburg, Cologne, Munich, Nuremberg, Regensburg and Stuttgart.
Police said the extortionist may be trying to turn up the heat on the food giant with the latest letter and may not have actually poisoned any products this time.
"The perpetrator has made very clear in the past that he's in a position to contaminate," said Peter Oehm, a spokesman for police in Frankfurt who are coordinating the nationwide probe.
"This potential threat is probably enough for him and he's possibly only putting us under psychological pressure."

Authorities appealed to members of the public to return mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, coffee, cocoa, tea and chocolate bought since (corrects from before) August 1 bearing the Thomy or Nestle brand names to police stations for examination.

The German Confederation of Retailers (HDE) said grocery stores had to deal with two or three extortion attempts every week. In around 75 percent of the cases, the extortionists did not try to pursue their claim after the first attempt.
HDE spokesman Thomas Werz said no one in Germany had so far been harmed by deliberately contaminated food.
